components.note: Originally depicted a hand 扌 gripping a weapon 戈; this original meaning was later borrowed to represent the pronoun 'I/we.'
亻 (person) — 们 attaches to pronouns and nouns referring to people to mark plural, e.g. 我们 ('we'), 你们 ('you all')
门 (mén) gives a sound close to 们's reading (men)

example.english: We are good friends.
example.fact: 们 attaches only to pronouns and words for people (我们, 你们, 朋友们) to mark plural — it can never attach to an ordinary object noun, so "books" is never 书们; Chinese instead relies on context or a number + measure word for object plurals.

components.note: 亻 (person) — 什 originally referred to a group of people.
十 (ten) — combined with 亻 (person), 什 originally described a group of ten; the character later came to be used for the common word 什么 (what).

example.english: What are you eating?
example.fact: 什么 pairs with 都 (什么都可以, "anything is fine") to mean "anything at all" — one of several question words (谁, 哪里, 什么时候) that flip from a question word into an "any-" word simply by adding 都 after it.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 知 relates to speaking what one knows.
矢 (shǐ) gives a hint of the sound — 知 is pronounced zhī, a connection that has faded over time.
辶 (to walk) — 道 relates to a path or road one walks along.
首 (shǒu) is the historical phonetic element; its modern reading no longer resembles dào, a reminder that sound components can drift after thousands of years of pronunciation change.

example.pinyin: Wǒ bù zhīdào tā de míngzi.
example.english: I don't know his name.
example.fact: 知道 ("to know" a fact or piece of information) is a common trap for English speakers, who have only one verb "to know" — Chinese requires 认识 instead for knowing a person, place, or being acquainted with something (认识他 "to know him", never 知道他).

components.note: 亻 (person) plus 也 (also/additionally) — historically meant 'another person,' which developed into the third-person pronoun 'he/him.'
亻 (person) — 们 attaches to pronouns and nouns referring to people to mark plural, e.g. 我们 ('we'), 你们 ('you all')
门 (mén) gives a sound close to 们's reading (men)

example.english: They are studying in the library.
example.fact: Chinese had no gendered third-person pronoun at all until the early 20th century, when 她 (with the 女 radical) was introduced under the influence of Western literary translation to distinguish "she" from "he" — 他们 as the default, mixed-gender "they" still reflects that older, ungendered system.

components.note: A single horizontal stroke — the simplest possible way to represent the number one; some traditional interpretations link it to heaven or earth as the very first stroke of creation.
丨 (a vertical tally mark) over 人 (person) — suggests counting people one by one, fitting 个's role today as Mandarin's most common general measure word.

example.pinyin: Zhuōzi shàng yǒu yí gè píngguǒ.
example.english: There is an apple on the table.
example.fact: 个 is Mandarin's default "general" measure word — when a noun's own specific classifier is unknown, forgotten, or simply doesn't exist, 个 is always a safe substitute, making 一个 one of the first and most reusable phrases a learner picks up.

components.note: 亻 (person) plus 尔 (an old second-person pronoun) — combines to form 你, the modern word for 'you.'
亻 (person) — 们 attaches to pronouns and nouns referring to people to mark plural, e.g. 我们 ('we'), 你们 ('you all')
门 (mén) gives a sound close to 们's reading (men)

example.english: What would you all like to drink?
example.fact: English "you" is ambiguous between one person and a group, but Mandarin marks the distinction explicitly: 你 is always singular and 你们 is always plural, with no equivalent gap the way English relies on context or "you guys".

components.note: 氵 (water) — 没 originally meant to sink or drown in water, later extended to the negative 'not have.'
殳 (shū) is the historical sound component; it no longer rhymes with méi in modern Mandarin, another case of sound drift over time.
月 (yuè) here actually derives from 肉 (meat) — 有 originally depicted a hand holding meat, meaning 'to possess'; it also lends a loose phonetic connection to yǒu.

example.english: There's no milk left in the fridge.
example.fact: 没 is the one verb that can negate 有 ("to have/there is") — Mandarin's everyday negator 不 cannot be used here (不有 is simply wrong), which is why 没有 has to be learned as its own fixed negation rather than 不 plus 有.

components.note: 丨 (a vertical tally mark) over 人 (person) — suggests counting people one by one, fitting 个's role today as Mandarin's most common general measure word.

example.english: This idea is very good.
example.fact: 个 itself, per its own etymology, depicts a tally mark stacked over 人 (person) — a picture of counting people one by one. 这个 simply attaches that default counter to the demonstrative 这 ("this") so it can stand alone as a pronoun, the same pattern behind 那个 ("that one") and 哪个 ("which one").

meanings: variant of 怎麼|怎么[zen3 me5]

components.note: 心 (heart/mind) — 怎's meaning 'how' relates to a mental inquiry, what's on one's mind.
乍 (zhà) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from zěn.

example.english: How do you pronounce this character?
example.fact: 怎么 alone asks "how" as an adverb before a verb (怎么念 "how do you read it"), while its close relative 怎么样 asks "how is X / how about X" as a stand-alone question about quality or status — a common point where beginners conflate the two.

components.note: 王 (a variant of 玉, meaning jade) — a valuable object one might glimpse or notice.
见 (to see) — catching sight of something links to the meanings 'to appear, present, now.'
土 (earth/soil) — 在 originally related to standing on the ground
才 (cái) gives the sound — 在 is pronounced zài, a close match

example.english: What time is it now?
example.fact: 现 (built from 见, "to see", catching sight of something) plus 在 ("to be present, at") combine almost literally as "what is manifesting, present" — giving 现在 its meaning "now, at present" through a fairly transparent compositional image.

components.note: 丁 (a stylized handle/hook shape in the ancient form) — part of the character's original picture, now mostly opaque in the modern form
口 (kǒu, mouth) gives a sound related to 可's pronunciation kě, and may connect to 可's sense of approval spoken aloud

example.english: May I come in?
example.fact: Chinese splits English "can" three ways: 可以 for permission ("is it allowed"), 会 for a learned skill ("do you know how"), and 能 for physical or circumstantial ability ("are you able to right now") — a three-way distinction with no single English equivalent.

components.note: 女 (woman) — depicts a wife in the traditional image behind this character.
口 (mouth/words) — the wife following her husband's spoken words gave 如 its meaning of 'as, like, if.'
田 (here representing round fruit, not its usual meaning 'field') — 果 pictures fruit hanging from branches.
木 (tree) — fruit growing on a tree gave 果 its meaning 'fruit' and, more broadly, 'result.'

example.hanzi: 如果明天下雨,我们就不去了。
example.pinyin: Rúguǒ míngtiān xiàyǔ, wǒmen jiù bú qù le.
example.english: If it rains tomorrow, we won't go.
example.fact: 如 (from 女 "woman" + 口 "mouth" — a wife following her husband's spoken word, hence "as, like") and 果 (fruit hanging from 木 "tree", hence "result") combine almost literally into "as the result [would be]" — a vivid compositional image underlying the everyday word for "if".

components.note: 木 (tree/wood) — 样 originally referred to a kind of tree, later broadening to mean 'kind, appearance, way.'
羊 (yáng) gives the sound — 样 is pronounced yàng, matching aside from tone.

example.english: Don't say it like that.
example.fact: 这样 modifies *how* an action is carried out, usually right before a verb (这样做, "do it this way") — its near-synonym 这么 (also in this batch) more often modifies *degree* right before an adjective (这么好, "this good"), a distinction English's single word "this" doesn't make.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — the act of speaking.
牛 (ox) — traditionally read as speaking with the forceful weight of an ox, giving 告 its meaning 'to tell, announce, inform.'
讠 (speech) — represents words being spoken.
斥 (to reprimand, blame) — words of accusation or complaint gave 诉 its meaning 'to sue, to tell, to complain.'

example.hanzi: 请告诉我你的电话号码。
example.pinyin: Qǐng gàosu wǒ nǐ de diànhuà hàomǎ.
example.english: Please tell me your phone number.
example.fact: 告诉 always names the listener directly after the verb (告诉 + person + thing, e.g. 告诉我 "tell me") — English "tell" can drop the listener, Chinese can't. Dictionaries also list a separate, fully-toned reading gàosù for a rarer legal sense, "to file a (private criminal) complaint" — the same two characters, a different register entirely.

example.pinyin: Wǒ méi qù, yīnwèi wǒ shēngbìng le.
example.english: I didn't go, because I was sick.
example.fact: 因为 almost always shows up paired with 所以 (also in this batch, at rank 36) in the fixed construction "因为...,所以..." — where English would find "because...so..." together in one sentence redundant, Chinese speech very often keeps both halves.

components.note: A picture of a nose; because people in ancient China would point to their own nose when referring to themselves, the character came to mean 'self.'
己 is thought to depict a woven cord or thread pattern, though its exact original picture is debated; it came to be used for the reflexive idea of 'oneself.'

example.hanzi: 她喜欢自己一个人旅行。
example.pinyin: Tā xǐhuan zìjǐ yí gè rén lǚxíng.
example.english: She likes traveling by herself.
example.fact: 自 is a pictograph of a nose (people in ancient China pointed to their own nose to mean "me"), and 己 separately depicts a woven cord, also borrowed for "self" — 自己 doubles up two originally independent "self" pictographs into one intensified reflexive word.

meanings: variant of 這裡|这里[zhe4 li3]

components.note: 田 (farmland) over 土 (earth/soil) — originally referred to a village or a measured unit of farmland, later extended to mean 'inside' or a unit of distance.

example.english: We'll wait for you here.
example.fact: 这里 (zhèlǐ) is the neutral, Mainland-standard word for "here"; Beijing-area speech commonly prefers the r-suffixed 这儿 (zhèr) instead, and Taiwan/Hong Kong writing uses 這裡 with the traditional 裡 — three regional flavors of the same word.

components.note: 旦 (dàn) gives the sound — 但 is also pronounced dàn, an exact match.
Traditionally analyzed as 日 combined with 疋, linked to the idea of speaking directly and truthfully — the source of 是's meaning 'to be, indeed, right.'

example.hanzi: 这件衣服很贵,但是我很喜欢。
example.pinyin: Zhè jiàn yīfu hěn guì, dànshì wǒ hěn xǐhuan.
example.english: This piece of clothing is expensive, but I really like it.
example.fact: 但是 sits at the neutral, standard-register end of Chinese's "but" words — 可是 feels a shade more conversational, and 不过 is the softest and most casual of the three near-synonyms — useful to know when picking which "but" fits the tone of a sentence.

components.note: 日 (sun/day) — relates to 时's meaning of 'time, season'; the phonetic part of the character was later replaced by 寸 in the simplified form
亻 (person) — relates to 候's meaning 'to wait, time,' as if a person watching and waiting.
矦 (hóu) gives a sound hint — 候 is pronounced hòu, sharing the same rhyme with a different tone.

example.pinyin: Xiǎo de shíhou, wǒ zhù zài Shànghǎi.
example.english: When I was little, I lived in Shanghai.
example.fact: 时候 almost always appears inside the frame "...的时候" ("at the time when...") attached to a preceding clause, functioning like an English "when"-clause marker — for freestanding "time" as a concept or duration, Chinese instead reaches for 时间 (also in this batch, at rank 42).

components.note: 纟 (silk/thread) — 经 originally referred to the vertical warp threads in weaving.
工 (gōng) gives a related sound cue for 经 (jīng), reflecting an older, closer pronunciation link between the two.

example.english: He has already left.
example.fact: 已经 is almost always paired with the sentence-final particle 了 to mark that something is complete ("已经...了"), much like English pairs "already" with a perfect-tense verb ("has already left") — a reliable pattern to reach for when building an "already" sentence.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 谢 describes an act of speaking, giving thanks.
射 (shè) gives the sound — an exact match with 谢.
讠 (speech) — 谢 describes an act of speaking, giving thanks.
射 (shè) gives the sound — an exact match with 谢.

example.english: Thank you for the gift.
example.fact: 谢谢 is just 谢 ("to thank") reduplicated — doubling a single-syllable verb is a common Mandarin device that softens and formalizes it, the same pattern behind 看看 ("take a quick look") and 试试 ("give it a try").

components.note: 亻 (person) — 什 originally referred to a group of people.
十 (ten) — combined with 亻 (person), 什 originally described a group of ten; the character later came to be used for the common word 什么 (what).

example.english: Why are you late?
example.fact: 为 ("for the sake of, because of") plus 什么 ("what") combine transparently into "for what [reason]" — unlike many Chinese question words, its literal logic maps almost directly onto the English phrase, making it one of the easier compounds to see through.

components.note: 见 (to see, perceive) — relates to 觉's meaning 'to feel, sense, perceive.'
⺍ is a small graphic element serving as the phonetic hint, though its link to jué's modern sound has faded after centuries of change.
寸 (a hand) reaching for 旦 (originally 貝, a shell used as currency) — a picture of grasping something valuable, hence 'to obtain, to get.'

example.hanzi: 我觉得这个电影很有意思。
example.pinyin: Wǒ juéde zhège diànyǐng hěn yǒu yìsi.
example.english: I think this movie is very interesting.
example.fact: 觉得 introduces a subjective feeling or impression ("I feel/think that..."), while its more formal cousin 认为 is reserved for a reasoned belief or judgment — in everyday speech 觉得 dominates, while 认为 shows up far more in writing, debate, or argument.

meanings: variant of 這麼|这么[zhe4 me5]

example.english: Why is the weather so hot?
example.fact: 么 is a recurring, toneless "helper syllable" that turns a root into a full colloquial word — the same 么 shows up in 什么 ("what"), 怎么 ("how"), and 那么 ("like that"), all also in this batch, forming a whole family of "-么" words built the same way.

components.note: 止 (a foot, stepping forward) — 先 pictures someone moving ahead of another.
儿 (a person) — one person stepping ahead of another gave 先 its meaning 'before' or 'first.'
屮 (a young shoot) growing up out of 土 (earth/soil) — a picture of new life emerging from the ground.

example.pinyin: Wáng xiānsheng, hěn gāoxìng rènshi nǐ.
example.english: Mr. Wang, nice to meet you.
example.fact: 先生 literally means "one born before" (先 "before" + 生 "born") — originally an honorific for a teacher or elder, someone who came before you in age or learning. It broadened over time into today's generic "Mr./sir", while still surfacing as "teacher" in some contexts.

components.note: 壴 (a drum) — beating a drum in celebration
口 (mouth) — singing along in celebration

example.english: I like drinking tea.
example.fact: 喜 already means "joy" on its own (built from 壴, a drum, plus 口, a mouth — a picture of singing and drumming in celebration), and 欢 separately means "happy, joyous" — 喜欢 doubles up two near-synonymous "joy" characters, a common Chinese strategy for building a two-character word.

components.note: 丁 (a stylized handle/hook shape in the ancient form) — part of the character's original picture, now mostly opaque in the modern form
口 (kǒu, mouth) gives a sound related to 可's pronunciation kě, and may connect to 可's sense of approval spoken aloud
Originally a drawing of a bear, with 厶 as its head, ⺼ as its body, and 匕匕 as its claws; the picture was later borrowed to mean 'ability, to be able to.'

example.english: It might rain tomorrow.
example.fact: 可能 does double grammatical duty as both an adverb ("maybe", before a verb) and a noun ("possibility", as in 可能性) — English usually needs two separate words, "maybe" and "possibility", to cover the same ground.

components.note: 雨 (rain) — something crops require to grow, giving 需 its meaning 'to need, require.'
女 (woman) with 覀 depicting hands on the waist — an old image of insisting or demanding something, connected to 要's meaning 'to want, to need.'

example.pinyin: Wǒ xūyào gèng duō de shíjiān.
example.english: I need more time.
example.fact: 需要 sits in the middle of a want/need/must spectrum: 要 alone can mean a plainer "want", 需要 is the neutral "need", and 必须 is reserved for a stronger "must" — useful for calibrating how urgent a request sounds.

components.note: Traditionally analyzed as 日 combined with 疋, linked to the idea of speaking directly and truthfully — the source of 是's meaning 'to be, indeed, right.'

example.english: "Are you a student?" "Yes, I am."
example.fact: 是的 is a softer, more polite affirmative than a bare 是 — appending 的 turns the blunt copula "is/am" into a gentler stand-alone answer particle for confirming a question, sitting a notch more courteous than the flatter, more abrupt 对 ("correct").

example.hanzi: 你想去,那么我们就一起去吧。
example.pinyin: Nǐ xiǎng qù, nàme wǒmen jiù yìqǐ qù ba.
example.english: If you want to go, then let's go together.
example.fact: 那么 mirrors 这么 (also in this batch) but points away from the speaker ("that much/so") rather than toward something close at hand — 那 vs. 这 is Mandarin's core far/near demonstrative pair, and nearly every demonstrative compound in this batch (那个/这个, 那么/这么) inherits the same contrast.

meanings: (used before a verb or adjective for emphasis)

components.note: 丨 (a vertical tally mark) over 人 (person) — suggests counting people one by one, fitting 个's role today as Mandarin's most common general measure word.

example.english: Who is that person?
example.fact: Beyond its literal use, 那个 (nàge) is one of Mandarin's most common hesitation fillers, like English "um" or "that thing" — and, as its own dictionary entry notes, it also serves as a euphemism for menstruation or sex in certain contexts, much as English reaches for vague stand-ins ("that time of the month") to avoid naming something directly.

components.note: 东 (simplified from 東) originally pictured the sun 日 rising behind a tree 木 — since the sun rises in the east, the character came to mean 'east.'
西 is thought to depict a bird settling into its nest at dusk — since birds return to roost as the sun sets in the west, the character came to mean 'west.'

example.pinyin: Wǒ yào qù shāngdiàn mǎi dōngxi.
example.english: I'm going to the store to buy things.
example.fact: A popular (though linguistically disputed) folk etymology traces 东西 ("thing") back to old market culture, where goods were sold from stalls clustered along a street's east and west sides — so "going to buy east-west" came to mean "going to buy things". Note the tone shift: dōngxī (both syllables toned) is the literal "east and west", while dōngxi (neutral second syllable) is the everyday noun "thing".

components.note: 讠 (speech) — relates to 该's meaning 'ought to, should,' as if reached through spoken agreement.
亥 (hài) gives a sound hint — 该 is pronounced gāi, sharing the same rhyme though the initial consonant and tone differ.

example.english: You should drink more water.
example.fact: 该 alone already means "should, ought to" (as in 该不该, "should or shouldn't"), while 应 separately contributes a sense of "corresponding to what's fitting" — 应该 reinforces two near-synonymous halves into one word, the same word-building strategy seen in 喜欢 (also in this batch).

components.note: 子 (child) — 孩 relates directly to children
亥 (hài) gives a sound close to 孩's reading hái
A simple drawing of a swaddled baby — arms reaching out, legs bundled together in a wrap.

example.pinyin: Zhè duì fūqī yǒu liǎng gè háizi.
example.english: This couple has two children.
example.fact: 子 on its own is a pictograph of a swaddled baby (arms out, legs wrapped), and 孩 combines the "child" element 子 with the phonetic 亥 (hài) for its sound — 孩子 pairs a full meaning-bearing root with a suffix character that itself still independently means "child", a case where the suffix's shift from full word to light grammatical ending is unusually easy to see.

components.note: 走 (to walk/run) — 起 relates to standing up and setting into motion.
己 (jǐ) gives a close sound cue — 起 is pronounced qǐ, sharing the same final sound.
Originally depicted a wheat plant; this agricultural picture was borrowed early on to represent the unrelated verb 'to come.'

example.english: Everyone, please stand up.
example.fact: Beyond its literal sense "to get up", 起来 is one of Mandarin's most productive verb-complement suffixes: attached after almost any verb it can mean "starting to..." (哭起来, "start crying"), "up off the ground" (拿起来, "pick up"), or "in the process of assessing" (说起来, "speaking of which") — several distinct extended senses layered onto one suffix.

components.note: 户 (door) — 所 evokes a location or place, such as where a door stands.
斤 (axe) — combined with 户 (door), the image of an axe at a door gave rise to the abstract sense of 'a place' or 'that which.'

example.hanzi: 下雨了,所以我们没去公园。
example.pinyin: Xiàyǔ le, suǒyǐ wǒmen méi qù gōngyuán.
example.english: It rained, so we didn't go to the park.
example.fact: 所以 is the fixed second half of "因为...,所以..." (also flagged at rank 15 in this batch) — where English speakers feel that using both "because" and "so" together sounds redundant, Chinese not only permits but favors keeping both halves in speech, though formal writing sometimes drops one.

components.note: 二 (two) — 些 originally suggested a small plural amount, building on the idea of 'more than one.'
此 (cǐ) is the historical phonetic element; it no longer closely matches the modern reading xiē.

example.pinyin: Zhèxiē shū dōu shì wǒ de.
example.english: These books are all mine.
example.fact: 些 is Mandarin's built-in marker for a small, indefinite plural ("some, a few"), so 这些 is literally "this + some" — swapping in 那 or 哪 gives 那些 ("those") and 哪些 ("which ones"), the same plural-marking job that 们 does for personal pronouns, just for demonstratives instead.

components.note: 辶 (to walk/move) — relates to motion or progress.
不 (not) — 'not yet moving on' gave 还 its meaning of 'still, yet.'
月 (yuè) here actually derives from 肉 (meat) — 有 originally depicted a hand holding meat, meaning 'to possess'; it also lends a loose phonetic connection to yǒu.

example.english: There's still some fruit in the fridge.
example.fact: 还 carries a core sense of "still, yet" that recurs across a whole family of common words (还是 "still/or", 还没 "not yet") — 还有 simply attaches that "still" sense to 有 ("to have") to get "there still is/remains", and spotting 还's recurring meaning helps a learner parse the whole family at once.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 问 relates to speaking, specifically asking a question.
门 (mén) gives a hint of the sound — 问 is pronounced wèn, related but the tone and vowel have shifted.
页 (head/page) — 题 relates to the forehead or the topmost part, extending to the 'title' or 'topic' placed at the top.
是 (shì) gives a hint of the sound — 题 is pronounced tí, a connection that has shifted over time.

example.pinyin: Wǒ yǒu yí gè wèntí xiǎng wèn nǐ.
example.english: I have a question I want to ask you.
example.fact: 问题 covers both a neutral "question" and a negative "problem" in one word, where English usually splits the two — which is why 没问题 (literally "no question") is the standard, extremely common way to say "no problem, that's fine", best learned as a fixed phrase rather than translated piece by piece.

components.note: A single horizontal stroke — the simplest possible way to represent the number one; some traditional interpretations link it to heaven or earth as the very first stroke of creation.
走 (to walk/run) — 起 relates to standing up and setting into motion.
己 (jǐ) gives a close sound cue — 起 is pronounced qǐ, sharing the same final sound.

example.english: Let's do homework together.
example.fact: 起 carries a core sense of "to rise, to arise" (as in 起来, also in this batch, and 起床 "to get out of bed") — 一起 literally combines "one" with "rise", an old image of several things "rising as one" that gave the word its modern sense, "together".

components.note: 廾 (two hands) — depicts hands at work.
一 represents the latch or bar of a door; hands lifting it away gave 开 its meaning 'to open, to start.'
女 (woman) — 始's meaning 'beginning' has been linked to the idea of the origin of life.
台 (tái) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from shǐ.

example.english: What time does the movie start?
example.fact: 开 pictures two hands (廾) lifting away a door's latch (一) — the act of "opening" something shut — while 始 is traditionally linked to 女 ("woman") as a source of origin. 开始 pairs "to open" with "to originate" into a vivid literal image of throwing open a beginning.

components.note: 日 (sun/day) — relates to 时's meaning of 'time, season'; the phonetic part of the character was later replaced by 寸 in the simplified form
门 (door/gate) — 间 pictures light passing through an entryway.
日 (sun) — sunlight shining through a gap in a doorway gave 间 its meaning of a space 'in between,' as in 中间 (in the middle) or 时间 (time, the space between moments).

example.english: We don't have time anymore.
example.fact: 时间 names time as a general concept or duration (没有时间 "no time"), while its near-synonym 时候 (also in this batch, rank 19) marks one specific moment and almost always sits inside a "...的时候" clause. 间 itself contributes a spatial sense of "a space between" — literally, 时间 frames time as the gap between moments.

components.note: 工 depicts a carpenter's square or workman's tool — a simple shape that came to represent work and labor.
亻 (person) plus 乍 (suddenly/for the first time) — together suggesting a person making or doing something for the first time.

example.pinyin: Tā měitiān gōngzuò bā gè xiǎoshí.
example.english: He works eight hours every day.
example.fact: 工作 functions as both a verb ("to work") and a noun ("job, work") with no change in form at all — a common feature of Chinese words that switch grammatical role for free, where English sometimes needs an entirely different word ("to work" vs. "a job").

components.note: 灬 (fire) — 然 originally described burning; the meaning later shifted to 'so, correct' as 然 became a grammatical particle.
肰 (rán) gives the sound — 然 is also pronounced rán, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 我们先吃饭,然后去看电影。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen xiān chīfàn, ránhòu qù kàn diànyǐng.
example.english: We'll eat first, then go watch a movie.
example.fact: 然后 is the standard connector for sequencing actions, often paired with 先 ("first") as here — but in casual storytelling it's also notorious as a near-meaningless filler that Mandarin speakers chain sentence after sentence ("...然后...然后..."), much like English speakers lean on "so" or "and then" when narrating.

components.note: A single horizontal stroke — the simplest possible way to represent the number one; some traditional interpretations link it to heaven or earth as the very first stroke of creation.
木 (tree/wood) — 样 originally referred to a kind of tree, later broadening to mean 'kind, appearance, way.'
羊 (yáng) gives the sound — 样 is pronounced yàng, matching aside from tone.

example.hanzi: 这两个杯子看起来一样。
example.pinyin: Zhè liǎng gè bēizi kàn qǐlai yíyàng.
example.english: These two cups look the same.
example.fact: 一样 does its real work inside the comparison frame "A 跟/和 B 一样(+adjective)" ("A is the same as B", e.g. 我跟你一样高, "I'm as tall as you") — one of the core building blocks of Chinese comparison sentences, alongside 比 ("more than"), beyond its plain gloss of "same".

components.note: 忄 (heart) — 情 relates to feelings and emotions.
青 (qīng) gives the sound — 情 is pronounced qíng, a close match differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 我今天有很多事情要做。
example.pinyin: Wǒ jīntiān yǒu hěn duō shìqing yào zuò.
example.english: I have a lot of things to do today.
example.fact: 事情 covers abstract matters, affairs, and tasks — never a physical object. For a physical "thing" Chinese instead reaches for 东西 (also in this batch, rank 32); English "thing" blurs both senses into one word, but Chinese keeps the abstract/concrete split strict between these two very common nouns.

components.note: 尤 (particularly/outstanding) — relates to 就's sense of approaching or arriving at a particular point
京 (jīng, capital) gives a sound close to 就's pronunciation jiù
Traditionally analyzed as 日 combined with 疋, linked to the idea of speaking directly and truthfully — the source of 是's meaning 'to be, indeed, right.'

example.hanzi: 他就是我一直在等的人。
example.pinyin: Tā jiùshì wǒ yìzhí zài děng de rén.
example.english: He is exactly the person I've been waiting for.
example.fact: 就 on its own already carries an emphatic "precisely this and nothing else", which 就是 sharpens by attaching it to the copula 是 ("to be") — the resulting word is also used constantly as a stand-alone agreement particle in speech ("就是!", "Exactly!/Right!"), functioning almost like an interjection.

components.note: 户 (door) — 所 evokes a location or place, such as where a door stands.
斤 (axe) — combined with 户 (door), the image of an axe at a door gave rise to the abstract sense of 'a place' or 'that which.'
月 (yuè) here actually derives from 肉 (meat) — 有 originally depicted a hand holding meat, meaning 'to possess'; it also lends a loose phonetic connection to yǒu.

example.pinyin: Suǒyǒu de xuésheng dōu dào le.
example.english: All the students have arrived.
example.fact: 所有 meaning "all" almost always shows up with 都 later in the sentence ("所有...都...") — 所有 modifies the noun, but it's the adverb 都 that actually carries the "without exception" meaning on the verb, and dropping 都 after a 所有-phrase is a common, noticeable slip for English speakers used to "all" doing that job alone.

components.note: A single horizontal stroke — the simplest possible way to represent the number one; some traditional interpretations link it to heaven or earth as the very first stroke of creation.
A short stroke placed below a longer one — the mirror image of 上 (up), together forming a simple, opposite pair.

example.pinyin: Děng yíxià, wǒ mǎshàng jiù lái.
example.english: Wait a moment, I'll be right there.
example.fact: 一下 attached after a verb softens and shortens an action into "just a moment of verb-ing" (等一下 "wait a sec", 看一下 "take a quick look") — grammatically it works much like the verb-reduplication pattern behind 谢谢 (also in this batch), just built from a numeral phrase instead of repeating the verb.

components.note: Depicts two things splayed apart from each other — such as a bird's two wings, or two people standing back-to-back — later used for the meaning 'not, contrary to.'
巾 (cloth) — 常 originally referred to a long skirt or banner made of cloth, later coming to mean something 'usual' or 'ordinary.'
尚 (shàng) gives a hint of the sound — 常 is pronounced cháng, a connection that has drifted over time.

example.english: This dish is extremely delicious.
example.fact: 非常 is a stronger, slightly more formal-sounding intensifier than the near-obligatory 很 ("very") that defaults before almost any adjective in a plain statement — reaching for 非常 in every single sentence, where a native speaker would just use 很, is a common tell of a learner overusing the "big" word for "very".
